passage.text: On Saturday, Malik visited the Fix-It Fair at the community center with his grandfather.
Tables held a lamp with a loose switch, a backpack with a torn strap, and a bicycle light that would not turn on.
Mr. Ortiz told the volunteers that they would salvage any parts that still worked.
Malik first thought salvage meant throwing things away.
Then he watched a volunteer save the light's clear cover and tiny screws for another repair.
He measured the torn strap before cutting a patch.
Mr. Ortiz reminded him to be precise: a patch that was even a little crooked could pull the strap out of shape.
Malik marked the fabric twice, then stitched slowly along the line.
Next, he used a sturdy clip from a broken key ring to hold the loose end in place.
The clip did not bend when he tugged it, so he knew it was strong enough for daily use.
At the end of the fair, Malik carried the backpack to its owner.
He had not made it look brand-new, but it was useful again.
He also understood why the volunteers kept a tray of saved parts: careful repairs can give ordinary objects another job.

questions.prompt: What does salvage most likely mean as Mr. Ortiz uses it?

choices.text: to save useful parts for another purpose
to throw away every broken object
to make an object look brand-new
to borrow tools from a neighbor

questions.explanation: After Malik hears the word salvage, he sees a volunteer save a clear cover and screws for another repair. That action shows that salvage means keeping useful parts.
